## Paper

## Abstract

Self-powered ferroelectric photodetectors offer an attractive platform for low-power optoelectronics, exploiting intrinsic bulk photovoltaic effects to achieve bias-free operation. However, their practical deployment has been hindered by slow temporal response and photocurrent drift, mainly due to inefficient thermal dissipation that leads to temperature buildup within the device under continuous illumination. Here, we report a thermal-diffusion-engineering approach that reconfigures the thermal environment of ferroelectric device to suppress lateral heat dissipation and enable efficient vertical heat extraction. Compared to conventional architecture, the engineered drift-free device exhibits a photoresponse speed improvement of over three orders of magnitude, along with complete drift suppression, enabling high-fidelity imaging with minimal crosstalk. Infrared thermography and COMSOL simulations confirm distinct thermal environment in conventional and drift-free devices, revealing strong heat accumulation in conventional and efficient heat extraction in drift-free architectures. This work highlights thermal diffusion engineering as a key device-design parameter for enhancing ferroelectric optoelectronic performance, paving the way for scalable, bias-free energy-harvesting photodetectors and neuromorphic imaging systems.

---

## Introduction

The rapid advancement of optoelectronics has driven interest in next-generation photodetectors featuring high sensitivity, broad spectral response, and long-term stability. Ferroelectric (FE) thin films have emerged as particularly attractive candidates because they can (i) generate a photovoltaic (PV) response without complex p-n junctions, (ii) produce a photovoltage that exceeds the bandgap, and (iii) enable a tunable output through mechanical, electrical, or magnetic control. This inherent coupling allows for tailored properties that enhance photovoltaic applications.

Among the range of potential FE materials, BiFeO3 (BFO) is specially compelling owing to its narrow bandgap (~2.7 eV), visible-light absorption, strong remnant polarization, intrinsic multiferroicity, and stable optoelectronic performance. These features collectively enable efficient carrier separation when illuminated due to its internal depolarization fields, thus supporting self-powered operation across the visible to near-ultraviolet spectrum The intrinsic room-temperature ferroelectricity of BFO renders it highly suitable for practical optoelectronic applications, including wearable imaging, optical communication, and neuromorphic computing.

Despite these advantages, the practical deployment of FE-based photodetectors has been hindered by persistent limitations, most notably a slow temporal response and photocurrent drift—defined as a gradual, unintended time-dependent variation in photocurrent when subject to continuous illumination. These limitations originate from illumination-induced heating and insufficient heat dissipation within the device. When the thermal environment is not well controlled, accumulated heat broadens the temporal response, reduces carrier extraction efficiency and destabilizes the steady state output. These thermally driven effects have been widely observed in oxide-based photodetectors, emphasizing that local heat distribution, is a critical but often overlooked determinant of device stability and dynamic performance.

Conventional FE photodetectors is commonly fabricated on low-thermal-conductivity substrates, such as mica or glass, with mica offering an atomically flat, chemically inert, and electrically insulating surface that is well suited for high-quality growth of perovskite oxide films. It also withstands high-temperature processing and provides mechanical flexibility, which has made it a standard platform for many BFO and related FE devices. However, its intrinsically low thermal conductivity leads to significant lateral heat accumulation during illumination, contributing to slow response and drift, and motivating our thermal-diffusion engineering strategy using high-k metallic backers. This phenomenon is conceptually related to thermal modulation transfer function (MTF) in pyroelectric imaging system, where lateral heat diffusion reduces the modulation depth and contrast of spatial signals. To improve the PV effect and overcome the associated challenges, recent strategies have focused on structural and electronic modifications. However, microscale thermal diffusion engineering remains an unexplored, but potentially transformative, approach for improving the dynamic performance of FE photodetectors.

Here we present a thermal diffusion engineering strategy that enables drift-free operation and fast temporal response in ferroelectric photodetectors by directing vertical heat extraction through a high conductivity copper substrate. Using BFO-based films as a model system, we demonstrate that thermal confinement suppresses lateral heat diffusion, thereby maintaining stable thermal environment under continuous illumination of light. Our optimized architecture demonstrates >3 orders of magnitude faster response speed and near-complete elimination of photocurrent drift compared to conventional devices. Infrared thermal imaging and COMSOL Multiphysics simulations confirm that the thermally conductive copper substrate is able to suppress lateral heat spreading and enhancing carrier mobility. Beyond fundamental performance gains, this thermally stabilized architecture also enables high-fidelity imaging with minimal crosstalk, positioning drift-free-FE devices as promising candidates for neuromorphic vision, wearable sensing, and next-generation optoelectronic systems requiring stable, precision operation.

---

## Results

Design of drift-free ferroelectric photodetector
A detailed comparison between conventional and drift-free photodetectors highlights how the thermal transport dynamics directly influence device performance and reveal distinct operational regimes. The conventional device structure consists of lanthanum nickelate (LaNiO3, LNO)/bismuth ferrite (BiFeO3, BFO)/indium tin oxide (ITO) on a mica substrate, consistent with previously reported FE photodetectors. The output signal characteristics reveal two fundamental limitations: a slow response time and notable photocurrent drift. The schematic elucidates the physical origin of these limitations: lateral thermal diffusion leads to in-plane heat spreading (circular isotherms) and causes thermal accumulation within the BFO layer which broadens the temporal response, producing the characteristic slow extraction and thermal drift.

The transformative improvement is achieved through our thermal engineering approach, where a high-thermal-conductivity copper layer is introduced beneath the mica substrate. This architecture yields a step-change in performance, eliminating photocurrent drift (blue arrow) and sharply reducing the response time (blue dotted rectangle). Vertical heat dissipation confines the local thermal gradients near the illumination site, suppresses lateral thermal spreading and maintains a stable thermal environment, which in turn enables drift free signal evolution.

This performance enhancement is quantitatively captured where the response time of the drift-free device outperforms conventional photodetectors by over three orders of magnitude, positioning our approach as a notable advancement in fast, stable FE optoelectronics.

Temporal and frequency-dependent photoresponse characteristics
When subject to pulsed illumination, the conventional BFO device exhibits a pronounced photocurrent drift, increasing from 39.13 to 121.04 μA during the illumination window; this represents a more than 200% increase in amplitude. This progressive rise reflects thermally activated charge accumulation, which produces artificial gain and delays carrier extraction. A magnified view of the rising edge reveals a sluggish response time of 1648 ms is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1a. These characteristics underscore the intrinsic bottlenecks in low-thermal-conductivity-supported FE photodetectors. In contrast, the Cu-backed device maintains a stable, drift-free photocurrent profile when subject to identical illumination conditions. The negligible difference between the initial and peak photocurrent values confirms the effective suppression of thermal buildup. A magnified view of the rising edge (Supplementary Fig. 1b) reveals a fast temporal response of 1.7 ms, which is nearly 1000 times faster than the conventional device, hereby validating the role of controlled thermal pathways in accelerating photocarrier dynamics.

The influence of illumination power density on response time is further elucidating the thermal management role. For both architectures the response time decreases with increasing power density. However, the conventional device’s response time (630–1648 ms) is consistently three orders of magnitude lower than that of the drift-free device (0.8–1.7 ms) across the measured illumination power density range. This vast difference underscores that the drift-free architecture, by providing a low thermal-resistance pathway, recovers the intrinsic electronic response time of the BFO layer. Recovery time trends (Supplementary Fig. 2) further confirm that it remains nearly illumination power-independent for both devices, with only a negligible increase at higher power densities. The millisecond-scale response time of the drift-free device is further substantiated by our frequency-domain analysis, where the extracted −3 dB bandwidth and corresponding phase lag fall within the 3–5 kHz range (Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. 3). Consistent with this bandwidth, a direct time-domain measurement at 100 Hz modulation yields a stable undistorted waveform and a response time of 0.25 ms (Supplementary Fig. 4), confirming operation in the kilohertz regime.

The gain behavior at low-frequencies (50 mHz − 10 Hz), further highlights crucial role of thermal management. The conventional device suffers a ~20% gain roll-off below 5 Hz, indicative of the system’s instability to reach the thermal equilibrium under modulated illumination. The drift-free device demonstrates exceptional stability with a gain variation of <5% across the same range. This flat frequency response is a direct consequence of the suppressed thermal time constant.

The gain power scaling of the two devices architectures, measured over illumination power density range of 80 mW cm−2 to 2.5 mW cm−2, reveals distinct thermal contributions to photocurrent generation. The conventional device exhibits a super-linear power-law dependance with a slope of 1.09, indicating that photocurrent increases faster than the incident photon flux. Such super-linearity is a well-known signature of thermally assisted carrier activation, where local temperature rise under continuous illumination enhances carrier population beyond direct photogeneration. In contrast, the drift-free device shows a near-linear scaling with a slope of 0.92 indicating that the photocurrent is governed primarily by direct photocarrier generation and extraction. The suppression of super-linear gain reflects efficient vertical heat dissipation, which prevents thermal accumulation and minimizes temperature-induced carrier amplification. This effective thermal management directly translates to improved figure of merits (FOM) for the drift-free device including lower noise current density, higher specific detectivity, and a superior signal to noise ratio (SNR), as detailed in the supporting information (Supplementary Note. 2 and Supplementary Figs. 7–12). The transition from super-linear to near-linear scaling thus provides direct evidence that thermal diffusion engineering effectively suppresses thermally driven gain enhancement and associated photocurrent drift.

To quantitatively validate the long-term stability of drift-free architecture, we performed systematic multi-hour and multi-day cycling experiments. Three independently fabricated devices were measured under identical modulated illumination (1 Hz, 405 nm, 1.6 W cm−2). Structural uniformity across these devices confirmed by SEM (Scanning electron microscopy) and AFM (Atomic force microscopy) (Supplementary Fig. 13, Fig. 14) shows consistent functional layers (BFO thickness: 66–73 nm; LNO thickness: 200–208 nm; RMS (root mean square) roughness: 1.09–1.24 nm) and lateral dimensions of 2×2 mm active area of all the devices. Each device exhibited the exceptional amplitude stability of 99.5–99.7% over continuous 2.7-h segments (Supplementary Fig. 15). To prove extended duration, one device was monitored for 41.6 h in sequential segments, maintaining >97% stability with no observable degradation in temporal waveform shape as shown in Fig. 2h. Furthermore, repeated measurements on different days confirmed robust reproducibility with stability consistently in the 99.3 to 99.5% range (Supplementary Fig. 16). This comprehensive dataset, supported by uniform structural parameters.

Figure 2i provides a comparative assessment of response times across a diverse set of FE photodetector systems, including BFO, lead titanate (PbTiO3, PTO), lead zirconate titanate (PbZr0.7Ti0.3O3, PZT), LNO, lead strontium tantalate (Pb0.8Sr0.2TaO3, PST), barium calcium titanate (Ba0.85Ca0.15TiO3, BCT), barium zirconium titanate (BaZr0.1Ti0.9O3, BZT), barium calcium zirconium titanate (Ba0.85Ca0.15Zr0.1Ti0.9O3, BCZT), barium titanate (BaTiO3, BTO), and barium strontium zirconium titanate (Ba0.8Sr0.2Zr0.1Ti0.9O3, BSZT), revealing a consistent performance enhancement in thermally engineered drift-free architectures (Supplementary Figs. 17, 18). All devices were fabricated and characterized in our laboratory under identical experimental conditions, using the same deposition method, electrode configuration, and a fixed active area of 2×2 mm, ensuring a fair and direct comparison across different material systems. Across all material platforms, drift-free devices exhibit accelerated temporal responses relative to their conventional counterparts, frequently exceeding improvements of one to two orders of magnitude. This consistent behavior underscores the thermal diffusion engineering as an effective and broadly applicable strategy for enabling fast photodetection in a wide spectrum of FE materials. This performance is against state-of-the-art ferroelectric photovoltaic (FE-PV) and pyro-phototronic photodetectors, with the results compiled in Supplementary Table 1, confirming the competitive advantage of drift-free architecture.

Thermal engineering for drift suppression
To definitively attribute the observed drift-suppression to thermal management rather than other artifacts, we conducted dark-state control experiments under controlled temperature conditions. First, dark thermal-pulse measurement shows no pyroelectric current in either the conventional or drift-free architecture (Supplementary Note. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 19). Second, temperature-dependent dark I-V characteristics are identical for both devices conventional and drift-free (Supplementary Note. 4 and Supplementary Figs. 20, 21), proving the Cu backer solely modifies the thermal boundary condition without affecting interfacial chemistry or intrinsic charge transport.

To comprehensively evaluate and quantify the photocurrent instability in FE photodetectors, we introduce the parameters of drift ratio and drift rate (Fig. 3a). The drift ratio ΔI/I1 quantifies the relative change in photocurrent from its initial (I1) to the peak (I2), capturing the extent of the time-dependent photocurrent, while the drift rate d(I/I1)/dt reflects the temporal gradients of this change. These metrics provide a robust framework for comparing photocurrent stability across devices with varying substrate properties and thermal configurations. A comparative analysis of drift ratio across devices supported on freestanding, thermoplastic, and metallic substrates reveals a striking contrast (Fig. 3b). Devices on thermoplastics and freestanding mica exhibit a substantial drift ratio (>150%), consistent with inefficient heat dissipation (see Supplementary Fig. 22). In contrast, devices integrated with metallic substrates exhibit near-complete suppression of drift ratio (<5%), highlighting the important influence of a high substrate thermal conductivity in stabilizing the FE photoresponse when illuminated. This trend is further reinforced, by examining the drift rate as a function of illumination time window (Fig. 3c) which reflects how quickly thermally induced photocurrent changes develop. The freestanding and thermoplastic-supported devices exhibit high drift rates, particularly at short illumination times, which gradually stabilize at longer durations (Supplementary Figs. 23–26). In contrast, the thermally conductive metallic substrates maintain consistently minimal drift rates across all time intervals, confirming effective suppression of thermal drift suppression (Supplementary Figs. 27–29). Optical absorption measurements confirm that the drift suppression is purely thermal, as all metallic backers (Cu. Al, SS) exhibit nearly identical absorption to the freestanding device; consistent with its minimal transmittance (0.6–1.7%), ruling out significant optical interference effects (Supplementary Note. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 30).

To establish a materials-level understanding of this behavior, we correlated the device drift characteristics with the intrinsic thermal conductivity of the supporting substrates (Fig. 3d). Thermoplastics exhibit thermal conductivities below 0.2 Wm−1 K−1, in contrast to metals, which exceed 100 Wm−1 K−1. This four-orders-of-magnitude disparity directly maps onto device performance. Experimental surface temperature measurements of each device subjected to 405 nm illumination (Fig. 3e) confirm this correlation (Supplementary Fig. 31). The conventional device without a heat sink reaches a temperature as high as 63 °C (ΔT≈38 °C above room temperature), indicating heat accumulation, whereas the copper-supported device remains closer to ambient (ΔT≈6 °C), signifying efficient vertical heat dissipation and reduced lateral spreading.

Infrared thermal imaging (Fig. 3f) of the devices visually confirms these trends. The conventional device exhibits isotropic lateral heat diffusion, forming broad circular hotspots that are fully consistent with lateral thermal diffusion and accumulation. In contrast the drift-free device backed with a copper substrate confines heat sharply at the illumination point, suppressing lateral thermal diffusion.

To theoretically validate these findings, we conducted computational simulations using the COMSOL Multiphysics software platform, specifically employing the Heat Transfer in Solids module (Fig. 3g). Time-dependent simulations using Fourier’s law capture heat transport in both freestanding and copper-integrated architectures. In the conventional stack, heat diffuses radially with increasing time, closely matching the experimental IR thermography data (Supplementary Fig. 32). In contrast, a copper-backed structure sustains a confined vertical heat plume with negligible lateral spread. Detailed COMSOL Multiphysics simulations, presented in Supplementary Note. 6 and and Supplementary Videos 1, 2, provide a comprehensive comparison of thermal behavior between the drift-free and conventional devices when subject to identical illumination conditions. The simulations (Supplementary Video 1) reveal that the conventional device undergoes a substantial temperature rise (63 °C) and exhibits thermal non-uniformity across the device area. In contrast, the drift-free device shows markedly lower temperature increase (32 °C) even at higher intensities and maintains uniform thermal distribution across its structure. Furthermore, Supplementary video 2 highlights that conventional device reaches the same temperature differential at much lower light intensities (0.9 W cm−2) compared to the drift-free device intensity (4.94 W cm−2), underscoring the superior thermal regulation enabled by the high thermal conductivity and diffusivity of the Cu substrate. These findings confirm the critical role of vertical heat extraction in suppressing local thermal accumulation and stabilizing device operation under continuous optical excitation.

Extending our analysis across a broad spectrum of thermally engineered FE materials (BFO, PTO, PZT, LNO, PST, BCT, BZT, BCZT, BTO, BSZT), we observe a consistent reduction in both drift ratio and drift rate compared to their conventional counterparts (Fig. 3h and Supplementary Fig. 17). These results highlight the general applicability of thermal diffusion engineering strategy, which effectively enhances temporal stability and suppresses thermally induced instabilities across diverse FE system.

Self-powered high-fidelity spatial imaging
High-fidelity spatial imaging is critical in modern electronic and optoelectronics systems, where precise detection, spatial localization of optical signals, and accurate mapping are essential for applications such as imaging sensors, optical communication, neuromorphic computing, and machine vision. However, achieving accurate spatial resolution in self-powered photodetectors is often hindered by lateral thermal diffusion, which introduces crosstalk between adjacent pixels or channels, distorting signal integrity. Here we demonstrate a schematic of the mode of device operation under selective illumination using a spatial mask, see Fig. 4a. Only a single channel of the device is exposed to light, while the neighboring channels are covered. In the conventional device, lateral thermal diffusion from the illuminated region results in spurious thermally induced voltage signals in the masked channels, thereby reducing spatial selectivity. In contrast, the drift-free device, which incorporates a thermally conductive copper substrate beneath the active layers, effectively limits lateral heat spread within the illuminated region. This thermal confinement prevents heat spread into adjacent areas, resulting in a clean, isolated voltage signal only from the exposed channel-highlighting the device’s superior spatial fidelity.

We also illustrate a conceptual design for a self-powered photodetector array used in imaging (Fig. 4b). A patterned light mask is projected onto the device, and the output voltage map is expected to reproduce the pattern with high accuracy. The experimental results using LabVIEW-based signal acquisition for photodetector arrays illuminated through “X” and “Z” shaped masks subjected to 405 nm light are provided (Fig. 4c). In the conventional devices, lateral heat conduction leads to detectable signals in the masked regions, blurring the spatial pattern. In contrast, the drift-free devices produce output signals that precisely match the illuminated shapes, confirming the suppression of thermal crosstalk and the ability to maintain sharp spatial boundaries between active and inactive regions. This superior spatial fidelity is quantitatively validated by a comprehensive analysis of channel crosstalk and the line-spread function (LSF), which show a seven-fold improvement in spatial confinement for the drift-free architecture (Supplementary Note. 7 and Supplementary Figs. 33–35). These findings establish the drift-free-FE photodetectors as a strong candidate for integration into spatially resolved optoelectronic systems, in particular where lower power consumption, fast response, and signal integrity are important. Further optimization, including systematic miniaturization to define the fundamental pixel-size-limits of this thermal-management strategy, presents a clear pathway for future high resolution imaging applications.

---

## Methods

Fabrication of LaNiO3 (LNO) bottom electrode
The LNO precursor solution was synthesized via sol-gel route. Ni(CH3COO)2·4H2O (nickel acetate-tetrahydrate) and La(NO3)3·6H2O (lanthanum nitrate-hexahydrate) were dissolved into a mixture of anhydrous ethanol and glacial acetic acid (molar ratio 1:1) under steady magnetic stirring at room temperature until a homogeneous light-green solution was obtained. The solution (LNO) was spin-coated onto freshly cleaved muscovite mica substrate (2000 rpm, 30s) using a programmable spin coater. Each deposited film was sequentially annealed at 200, 400, and 680 °C (3 min each) to remove organic residuals and crystallize the perovskite phase. This spin-coating and annealing cycle was repeated six times to achieve an LNO film with optimal conductivity and surface roughness.

Deposition of BiFeO3 (BFO) and other FE layers
A stoichiometric BFO precursor solution (0.2 mol L−1) was prepared by dissolving Bi(NO3)3·5H2O (bismuth nitrate pentahydrate) and Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (ferric nitrate nonahydrate) in ethylene glycol under ambient conditions. The solution (BFO) was spin-coated atop the LNO stack (4000 rpm, 30s), followed by stepwise pyrolysis at 180, 350, and 550 °C (3 min each) to ensure gradual organic removal and crystallization. The deposition cycle yielded a BFO film with uniform morphology. The methodologies for depositing other FE materials including PTO, LNO, PZT, PST, BCT, BZT, BCZT, BTO, and BSZT follow analogous spin-coating methods.

Integration of ITO (top electrode) and conventional device assembly
An array of 2×2 mm electrodes was patterned on the BFO surface using a shadow mask. The indium tin oxide (ITO) top electrode was deposited via RF magnetron (ZDF-5227 Composite Vacuum Gauge) sputtering (150 W, Ar Atmosphere, base pressure 4.5×10−6 Torr, 1200 s deposition time). Ohmic contacts were made by attaching copper wires to the ITO (top) and LNO (bottom) electrodes with conductive silver paste.

Drift-free device configuration
Freestanding devices were stacked onto different metallic and thermoplastic plates using a small amount of silver paste applied exclusively at the peripheral edges, ensuring no contact with electrodes or obstruction of the central active optical path. We prepared the other FE devices by following the same steps.

Device characterization and measurements. Photoresponse measurements were performed using a combination of a Keithley 6514 electrometer and Keithley 2611B source-meter for low-noise current detection and electrical characterization. For time resolved measurements, the photocurrent signal was amplified using a low-noise current amplifier (Stanford Research system SR570) with suitable sensitivity with respect to the intensity of light and recorded with a mixed-domain oscilloscope (Tektronix MDO3024). A low distortion function generator (Stanford Research system DS360) was used to modulate the laser intensity for frequency-dependent and transient response measurements. Calibrated laser source (MLL-III, DE52509) with wavelength 405 nm and power density of 320 mW cm−2 to 2.5 W cm−2 were employed, with the optical power monitored using a calibrated power meter (OPHIR PD300) (Supplementary Fig. 36).

For full frequency-response characterization, including gain and phase (Bode plots), a lock-in-amplifier (Stanford Research system SR865A) was employed.

Reflectance and transmittance spectra were measured using the OceanView Spectrophotometer equipped with a fiber-optic probe for the collection of reflected and transmitted light intensities, and the transmittance was further independently verified by using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer (Ultra 6600A).

For quantitative spatial metrics, including line-spread function (LSF) and crosstalk measurements, a microscope equid with a camera (TD-4KE) was used to focus the optical spot onto the device channel, while the sample was mounted on an x-y translational stage with micrometer-scale positioning accuracy to enable controlled scanning across the channel.

Temperature dependent I-V and transient measurements were carried out using a heating stage for temperature control, a Keithley 2260B source meter for voltage sourcing and a kiethely 6514 electrometer for high-sensitivity transient current recording.

Thermal Imaging: Transient temperature gradients during device operations were mapped using an Optris Xi 400 infrared thermal imager for both conventional and drift-free (with metallic substrate) devices.

Data acquisition: Voltage outputs were logged at the NI PXIe-1082 system with LabVIEW-based signal processing software. The measurements were conducted under the controlled illumination from a 405 nm light source, with optical patterning applied using two distinct mask shapes (Z and X). Data were collected for both conventional and drift-free device configurations to enable comparative analysis. All experimental parameters, including light intensity, sampling rate, and ambient conditions, were held constant across trials to ensure reproducibility.

Thermal Conductivity: Cross-plane thermal conductivity of individual layers was measured using a steady-state HS-DR-5 analyzer (error margin ±5%).

Simulations: To theoretically validate our experimental observations, we performed comprehensive 3D thermal simulations using COMSOL Multiphysics (v6.1) with the “Heat transfer in solids” physics interface. The simulations were designed to replicate the exact geometric and material conditions of both conventional and drift-free-FE photodetectors, enabling direct comparison with experimental thermal imaging data (Fig. 3f–g).

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Minhas et al. report “drift-free” ferroelectric photodetection with purported ultrafast response via thermal-diffusion engineering using a high-thermal-conductivity Cu backer. To this reviewer, the work is moderately original—the heat-sinking lever is evolutionary and known in thermal/pyro-detector design, but the systematic drift quantification (drift ratio/rate across materials) and the imaging/crosstalk demonstration are useful contributions. Several central claims remain insufficiently supported: the detector is not convincingly “ultrafast,” key detector figures of merit are missing, and the governing mechanism is not isolated. Overall, the manuscript sits at the boundary of acceptance; in its current form, I recommend rejection for Nature Communications. My specific comments follow.
(1) The manuscript highlights a 0.36 ms rise time (oscilloscope, Fig. 2d) and emphasizes “frequency-independent” response. However, the main-text frequency sweeps span only 0.1–1.5 Hz, and the Supporting Information extends to 300 Hz for different substrates, still without an explicitly reported −3 dB bandwidth or phase response. To substantiate the “ultrafast” claim, it is necessary to report full Bode plots (gain and phase versus frequency), the −3 dB point with confidence intervals, and noise spectra under matched optical and electrical conditions (same bias, area, illumination level, load, and temperature). Without these, the “ultrafast” characterization remains unsubstantiated.
(2) Most critical measurements are performed at 1-5 W cm-2 @ 405 nm, which are very high irradiances relative to many application regimes. The manuscript does not report basic photodetector figures of merit—responsivity (R), noise current, noise-equivalent power (NEP), and specific detectivity (D*)—nor does it analyze SNR versus flux. It is required to include these measurements to position the device credibly against standard photodetector baselines. These metrics are necessary for fair comparison and for assessing practical relevance.
(3) The thermal-diffusion narrative (IR thermography, COMSOL heat-flow modeling, substrate-dependent ΔT reduction) is persuasive but does not isolate the photovoltaic contribution from photothermal/pyroelectric effects. To support the claim that thermal engineering directly yields “drift-free” behavior, it is required to include the following controls: (i) dark thermal pulses (no light) to mimic ΔT transients and quantify purely thermal responses; (ii) multi-wavelength tests at equal absorbed power (not merely equal incident power), verified via reflectance/absorbance; (iii) temperature-ramp bias tests to track responsivity/drift metrics versus controlled substrate temperature; and (iv) matched-optics stacks on low-k vs high-k spreaders with identical optical interference conditions. These controls are necessary; without them, the assertion “drift-free via thermal engineering” remains plausible but not isolated from competing mechanisms.
(4) The manuscript asserts “universal effectiveness” across multiple ferroelectric materials but presents primarily exemplar curves. There is no report of device counts, error bars, distributions or yield, or long-term endurance beyond a single ≈3000 s trace. To support generality, it is necessary to provide, for each material/system, the sample size; spread for drift metrics and rise/decay times; yield statistics; and hour-to-day cycling data (including bias/temperature stress). These statistics must be included to elevate the claims from anecdotal to robust.
(5) The X/Z-mask demonstrations are visually illustrative but qualitative. To substantiate “high-fidelity imaging” and reduced crosstalk, the manuscript must include quantitative array-level metrics: crosstalk matrices (with nearest-neighbor leakage percentages), point-spread functions (PSF), modulation transfer functon(MTF), and per-pixel isolation maps derived from the 25-channel time traces. Reporting line-pair resolution and contrast versus spatial frequency is necessary. Without these quantitative measures, the imaging-centric claims remain insufficiently supported.
(6) Metal backers can alter optical absorption and interference (etalon effects), not merely thermal conduction. For fair isolation of thermal effects, it is required to equalize absorbed optical power (not just incident power) via measured reflectance/absorbance and to state the exact optical stack (layer materials, thicknesses, roughness) used in each comparison. Replotting key comparisons under matched absorbed power is necessary; otherwise, thermal and optical effects remain confounded.
(7) The manuscript repeatedly attributes trap suppression to vertical heat extraction through Cu (e.g., “reduced activation of trapping centers”) yet trapping/detrapping kinetics are primarily governed by the semiconductor and its interfaces—defect chemistry, interface states, and band alignment—while Cu chiefly modifies the thermal profile, not the trap spectrum. It is required to decouple thermal management from trap physics; this requires, for example, identical stacks on Fe/Al/Cu with matched thickness/roughness to separate thermal conductivity from work-function/optical changes; absorbed-power-matched multi-wavelength tests; and interfacial forensics to exclude Cu diffusion or unintended interlayers. The discussion must reconcile any observed leakage or power-law changes that could arise from barrier/interface modifications rather than cooling alone.
(8) The manuscript assigns an intensity exponent of 0.87 to space-charge-limited conduction with minimal recombination losses. However, an exponent <1 can also indicate trap-mediated recombination and other non-idealities. It is necessary to validate this interpretation via temperature-dependent and intensity-dependent exponent maps, transient rise/decay analyses, and contact-geometry controls (e.g., varying electrode work function or area). Without these corroborations, the SCLC assignment is not unique, and the mechanism remains ambiguous.
(9) Oscilloscopes measure voltage, not current. The manuscript does not document the sensing chain used to report current from the recorded voltages. It is required to include a clear measurement-circuit schematic and parameters. These details are necessary to interpret both the absolute current levels and the claimed temporal response.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents a novel thermal-diffusion engineering strategy for ferroelectric photodetectors, achieving a remarkable improvement in response speed (>10³×) and complete suppression of photocurrent drift. Studying is motivated, as slow dynamics and instability are long-standing challenges in self-powered FE devices. The combination of infrared thermography and COMSOL simulations provides convincing support for the proposed mechanism. Moreover, the architectural focus on controlling vertical versus lateral heat flow is original and complementary to the more common material/interface engineering approaches.
To further strengthen the impact and clarity of the work, I suggest the authors address the following points:
1. The manuscript claims a >10³× improvement in photoresponse speed, but absolute rise/fall times are not directly compared to state-of-the-art FE–PV and pyro-phototronic detectors. Please provide explicit numerical values (µs/ms scale) and include a benchmarking table against relevant literature.
2. While a >10³× speed improvement is reported, the manuscript does not present a comprehensive comparison of photoresponse speeds between FS-BFO and DF-BFO devices across a broad range of light intensities (from mW/cm² to W/cm²). Including this analysis would make the claims more rigorous.
3. Some data appear inconsistent across different figures. For example, in Fig. 2a the FS-BFO device shows a sharp initial rise in Isc followed by a gradual increase, whereas in Fig. 4a the conventional BFO device exhibits a sharp rise followed by a gradual decay. In Supplementary Figs. 24–25, FS-BFO shows a fast rise followed by a linear decay. These behaviors cannot all be explained by the model proposed in the main text. The authors should clarify these discrepancies.
4. Similar inconsistencies are observed for DF-BFO devices. In Fig. 2d, Isc increases linearly after the initial sharp rise; in Supplementary Fig. 24, it decreases linearly; and in Supplementary Fig. 25, it decreases non-linearly. The authors should provide a clear explanation for these variations.
5. Since pyroelectric and photovoltaic effects may coexist in BiFeO₃ and related ferroelectrics, please clarify whether the observed speed enhancement originates solely from reduced polarization screening, or if pyroelectric contributions also play a role.
6. Several relevant studies on pyroelectric/pyro-phototronic detectors are missing. Including these references would strengthen the discussion and provide a more balanced comparison.

### Reviewer 3

Minhas et al. report a simple yet highly effective strategy to overcome two persistent limitations of ferroelectric (FE) photodetectors: slow temporal response and photocurrent drift. By integrating BFO thin films on high-thermal-conductivity copper substrates, the authors demonstrate >1000x faster response times (0.36 ms vs. 1648 ms) and near-complete drift suppression compared to conventional freestanding devices. Infrared thermography and COMSOL simulations convincingly support the proposed mechanism of enhanced vertical heat extraction and suppressed lateral heat diffusion. The approach is shown to be broadly applicable across multiple FE materials and enables high-fidelity, low-crosstalk spatial imaging. The work addresses a significant bottleneck in FE optoelectronics, and the experimental data are persuasive. However, in the current state I cannot recommend publication. The manuscript would benefit from addressing the following points.
1. Page2, line60: “A common feature of conventional FE photodetectors is their fabrication on low-thermal-conductivity base materials such as mica or glass”. Why is this the common fabrication method and what advantages does this bring apart from the disadvantage of inefficient heat extraction. Since the authors themselves are also growing on mica.
2. Fig2g, 1h of measurement is neat, but to talk about long-term stability, it would be helpful if the device is measured also after 1 week or longer. Calling 1h of stability “unprecedented” is a bit of a far-fetched claim.
3. As stated in the manuscript, the devices exhibit a response time of only 0.36 ms, the bandwidth of the devices however is only measured until 1.4 Hz. That the DF device doesn’t even come near its limit, is quite trivial. With that response time, measurements into the kHz range should be possible. I encourage the authors to include higher frequency measurements.
4. Fig2i: when reading this paragraph, it was not very clear if the comparison data is experimental or not. Furthermore, I am missing a discussion on why exactly BFO is by far better than all the other oxides, namely two orders of magnitude and a relative increase between FS and DF of four orders of magnitude. Later in the manuscript it is mentioned that “While BFO-based DF devices exhibit the most pronounced improvements, attributed to their robust PV properties,…”, which needs further discussion.
5. Maybe trivial, but not mentioned, how are the devices fixed onto the metal substrates?
6. From a thermal management perspective, shouldn’t it be irrelevant how thick the copper substrate is once a minimum drift ratio is reached? It seems like the drift-ratio goes up again for thicker substrates than 0.8mm, which to me is counterintuitive. How many substrates have been included in that study per thickness?
7. The last section of the spatial detector array feels a bit like a small anecdote just repeating the advantages of the DF concept. Almost no practical parameters nor limitations for the use of the detector are discussed. The devices are quite big in terms of technological significance. The spatial imaging with “X” and “Z” masks is promising but relatively qualitative. Quantitative metrics like modulation transfer functon(MTF) or crosstalk ratio would be stronger. Covering the following questions would make this section more valuable for potential applications. How small can the array be made until crosstalk even for the DF architecture happens? 2mm pads are huge, what is the limit here? In that regard, from the methods section I understand, that to actually measure the device the ITO pads are directly contacted with silver paint (the device figure in S28 is shown without those contacts). Having to place the contact on top would probably significantly influence device miniaturization as incoming light gets blocked. What other approach would be necessary to deal with that issue?

Answer 5: We thank the reviewer for raising the possibility of pyroelectric contributions. We
performed the most direct and discriminating controls requested and report the results below. The
new data substantially isolates the photovoltaic contribution from photo-thermal/pyroelectric
effects and support the conclusion that thermal-diffusion engineering is the principal mechanism
that reduces photocurrent drift.
In ferroelectric photodetectors, polarization screening refers to the gradual compensation of
ferroelectric polarization charges by mobile carriers and defects, which weakens the internal field
and slows the photoresponse. In our devices, the ferroelectric layer, interfaces, and electrode
configuration are identical for conventional-BFO and drift-free-BFO; therefore, the intrinsic
polarization screening mechanisms are not modified by the Cu backer.
To distinguish photovoltaic and pyroelectric contributions, we performed dark thermal-pulse
experiments on our drift-free device. The drift-free device was subjected to different temperature
change and the corresponding currents were measured in Figure R30. The measured signals exhibit
only slow, monotonic rise and decay consistent with heating and cooling governed by the thermal
time constant of the device-substrate system. Importantly, no fast, polarity-reversing transient;
characteristic of pyroelectric current associated with dT/dt was observed. Therefore, our output
photoelectric signal does not contain a pyroelectric component but does exhibit a certain
thermoelectric contribution. However, the thermoelectric signal generated by a temperature change
of approximately 30 °C is only on the nano-ampere level (Figure R30), whereas the temperature
rise induced by illumination in our samples is only 6 °C yet produces a photocurrent of 106 µA
(Fig. 2d). Therefore, the output of our device is dominated by the photovoltaic signal, no pyro-
electric effect, and the minor thermoelectric component can be safely neglected.

Minhas et al. report a simple yet highly effective strategy to overcome two persistent limitations
of ferroelectric (FE) photodetectors: slow temporal response and photocurrent drift. By integrating
BFO thin films on high-thermal-conductivity copper substrates, the authors demonstrate >1000x
faster response times (0.36 ms vs. 1648 ms) and near-complete drift suppression compared to
conventional devices. Infrared thermography and COMSOL simulations convincingly support the
proposed mechanism of enhanced vertical heat extraction and suppressed lateral heat diffusion.
The approach is shown to be broadly applicable across multiple FE materials and enables high-
fidelity, low-crosstalk spatial imaging. The work addresses a significant bottleneck in FE
optoelectronics, and the experimental data are persuasive. However, in the current state I cannot
recommend publication. The manuscript would benefit from addressing the following points.
Comment 1: Page2, line60: “A common feature of conventional FE photodetectors is their
fabrication on low-thermal-conductivity base materials such as mica or glass”. Why is this the
common fabrication method and what advantages does this bring apart from the disadvantage of
inefficient heat extraction. Since the authors themselves are also growing on mica.
Answer 1: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Mica is indeed widely used as a
substrate for ferroelectric and oxide thin films, not only for convenience but because it offers
several well-documented materials advantages. First, its mechanical flexibility and high thermal
stability allow high-temperature oxide processing while enabling flexible or transferable device
architectures, which has motivated its widespread adoption in ferroelectric memories, sensors,
and photodetectors (Li et al., Nat. Commun., 2020; Liu et al., Adv. Funct. Mater., 2021) Second, mica
is chemically inert, optically transparent, and electrically insulating, making it particularly suitable
for self-powered ferroelectric photovoltaic and optoelectronic measurements without parasitic
leakage or substrate-induced screening (Zheng et al., ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces, 2018). Third,
mica provides an atomically flat, layered surface that enables van der Waals-assisted or quasi-
epitaxial growth of perovskite oxides, often resulting in reduced interfacial strain, low defect
density, and robust ferroelectric polarization (Wang et al., Adv. Mater., 2016; Ji et al., Nano Energy,
2019). Furthermore, mica enables mechanical flexibility while maintaining thermal and chemical
stability up to ~700 °C, making it attractive for flexible ferroelectric devices, including BFO and
PZT thin films (RSC Mater. Adv. 2022; J. Mater. Chem. C 2020). Recent ferroelectric memory
59
studies on BFO/mica stacks have also confirmed its good crystalline compatibility, fatigue
endurance, and mechanical robustness. These attributes explain why conventional FE
photodetectors including our own baseline conventional-BFO device are commonly fabricated on
mica. However, as the reviewer points out, its inherently low thermal conductivity remains a
drawback when fast response is required, and this is precisely the limitation our thermal-diffusion
engineering concept aims to overcome.

Answer 4: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the need for clarification regarding Fig. 2i and
the underlying physical origin of the observed performance differences. We would like to clarify
that all comparison data shown in Fig. 2i is based exclusively on our own experimental
measurements, rather than literature-derived values. All ferroelectric devices included in this
comparison were fabricated under identical processing conditions, including the same deposition
method (Sol-gel and spin coating), identical bottom (LNO) and top (ITO) electrode configurations,
and a fixed device active area of 2 mm × 2 mm. This controlled approach was intentionally adopted
to enable a direct and fair comparison of response speed and drift behavior across different
ferroelectric material systems within the same device architecture.
The order-of-magnitude differences observed in Fig. 2i should be interpreted in two distinct and
physically different contexts. First, when comparing different ferroelectric materials fabricated and
measured under identical device architectures, the BFO device exhibits an approximately one to
two-order-of-magnitude faster photoresponse than other ferroelectric oxides investigated in this
work. This superiority originates from intrinsic material properties of BFO, including its relatively
narrow optical bandgap (~2.5 - 2.8 eV), which makes it more responsive to visible illumination
compared to many wide-bandgap oxide ferroelectrics such as BaTiO or LiNbO . (Nat. Commu.
3 3
4, 2835 (2013)). This narrower bandgap, combined with robust spontaneous polarization, enables
significant ferroelectric photovoltaic response, as evidenced in multiple device studies where
photocurrent and photovoltage are strongly modulated under illumination. (ACS Appl. Mat. 10,
13712-13719 (2018)). The role of ferroelectric polarization and domain structures in facilitating
photovoltaic effects has been reported in BFO thin films, where polarization-modulated internal
fields significantly influence photovoltaic behavior. (Scie. Rep. 10, 15108 (2020)). Although not
directly related to this study, substantial photovoltaic effects and switchable behavior have been
demonstrated even in polycrystalline BFO films on transparent substrates, demonstrating that the
67
intrinsic photovoltaic properties of BFO are robust across different material forms (Thin Solid
Films 698, 137851 (2020)).

Answer 5: We thank the reviewer for this practical and relevant question. The devices were
mechanically fixed onto the metal substrates using a small amount of silver paste applied only at
the peripheral edges of the conventional device, well outside the active channel region. Care was
taken to ensure that the silver paste does not contact any electrodes, does not electrically short the
device, and does not obstruct the optical path during illumination. The central active area of the
device remains in direct physical contact with the metal substrate, enabling efficient vertical heat
extraction while preserving identical electrical and optical measurement conditions. To improve
clarity and reproducibility, we have now included a detailed description of the mounting procedure
in the Methods section.

Answer 6: We thank the reviewer for this insightful and technically important comment. We agree
that, from a thermal-management perspective, once the copper substrate exceeds a critical
minimum thickness, further increases should not significantly enhance heat extraction. Our
experimental results are fully consistent with this expectation.
In our study, we first compared conventional devices with thermoplastic-backed and metal-
backed devices using substrates of identical lateral dimensions and thickness. Among these, the
Cu-backed configuration exhibited the most effective drift suppression and fastest response, with
marginally better performance than Al or stainless-steel substrates. Subsequently, to examine
thickness dependence, we investigated 12 Cu-backed devices spanning eight different substrate
thicknesses. As anticipated, the variation in drift ratio and response time beyond a certain thickness
was extremely small, typically within 0.2 - 0.4% (Figure R36), which is negligible compared to
the substantial improvement achieved when transitioning from conventional or thermoplastic
supports to a metallic heat sink.
Because an overly narrow range was chosen in the original manuscript, the drift ratio at 0.8 mm
appeared visually unreasonable; however, in reality, the drift ratio at 0.8 mm is 0.58% which falls
within the range of 0.58% to 0.62% observed over the measured thickness range. The highly
zoomed scale used in previous version had visually amplified minor fluctuations that lie well
within experimental uncertainty and do not represent a physically meaningful trend. We apologize
for any confusion caused by the original presentation, and in the revised manuscript, we have
adopted a more appropriate y-axis scale in the Figure R36, clearly demonstrating that thickness-
induced variations are negligible once the optimal heat-extraction regime is reached. Overall, these
results confirm that the primary performance enhancement arises from the introduction of a high-
thermal-conductivity metal heat sink.

Answer 7: We thank the reviewer for this constructive and forward-looking comment.
The spatial imaging experiment with “X” and “Z” masks were performed using the device
geometries with a 2 mm × 2 mm active pad, with a light source of 405 nm under identical
illumination intensity for both freestanding and drift-free devices.
In the present work, our primary objective was to establish a clear, controlled comparison
between conventional and drift-free architectures, focusing specifically on photocurrent drift
suppression and response-speed enhancement enabled by vertical heat extraction. We fully agree
that investigating the minimum achievable pixel size and the onset of crosstalk in drift-free
architectures is an important next step. The active pad size of our BFO device is determined by the
area of top ITO electrode and can be readily reduced at least micro-meter scale by controlling the
sputtering mask and electrode contact dimensions. It can be a future research direction.
Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have strengthened this section by adding quantitative
spatial metrics using the most direct measurements accessible with our current instrumentation.
Specifically, we performed point-spread-function (PSF) derived line-spread function (LSF)
(Response Figure R37) by illuminated a focused optical spot (diameter ≈ 230 µm) across a single
2 mm × 2 mm channel at nine discrete lateral positions. For the conventional device, the
normalized signal drops to only ~48% at the edge of the channel, indicating a broad lateral
response halo consistent with strong in-plane thermal diffusion. In contrast, the Cu-backed drift-
free device exhibits a rapid signal decay to < 7% at the same lateral position, demonstrating a
sharply localized response and strongly suppressed lateral heat spreading.

Second, we constructed quantitative crosstalk matrices by selectively illuminating channel 13
and recording the time-resolved response of neighboring channels (Figure R38,39). In the
conventional device, the nearest-neighbor channels (12 and 14) exhibit 10 - 11% of the primary-

the drift-free device shows no measurable signal above the dark-noise floor in any adjacent channel,
corresponding to nearest-neighbor leakage below 1%. These results quantitatively confirm the
substantial suppression of array-level crosstalk achieved through thermal-diffusion engineering.
